slides.title: The Three Factors of Authentication

quiz.question: A banking site requires a password AND the answer to 'What was your first pet's name?' before login. Why does this NOT qualify as multi-factor authentication?
options: Security questions are always publicly guessable
Both controls are knowledge factors, something the user knows, so no second independent factor category is present
The site does not use HTTPS
Security questions require a hardware token
quiz.explanation: MFA requires combining factors from at least two distinct categories (knowledge, possession, inherence). A password and a security-question answer are both knowledge factors, so an attacker who has compromised one knowledge-based secret (e.g., via a data breach or social engineering) faces no additional independent barrier from the other.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Sets the taxonomy the rest of the topic builds on, every later slide maps back to one or more of these three categories.

Misconception: Students think any second login step is 'MFA.' Two knowledge factors (password + security question) is not true MFA.

Analogy: A bank vault requiring both a key (possession) and a combination (knowledge) is genuine two-factor; requiring two different combinations from the same dial is not.

Exam tip: If a scenario names two controls, check they come from different categories before calling it MFA.
bullets: Knowledge: Something you know, passwords, PINs, passphrases, security questions
Possession: Something you have, hardware keys, smart cards, authenticator apps
Inherence: Something you are, fingerprints, facial geometry, iris, voice, typing rhythm
MFA rule: Combining two factors from the SAME category is not MFA, two passwords is still one factor
Irreversibility asymmetry: A stolen password can be changed; a compromised fingerprint cannot

content_blocks: Every authentication scheme in modern computing reduces to some combination of three canonical factor categories. Knowledge factors are shared secrets, a password, a PIN, the answer to a security question, and their defining weakness is that a secret provides zero protection once an attacker knows it. Possession factors are physical objects, a hardware security key, a smart card, a phone running an authenticator app, that are far harder to steal remotely because they require physical access or theft of a specific device.

Inherence factors are biometric: fingerprints, facial geometry, iris patterns, even behavioral signals like typing cadence. Biometrics are convenient because they cannot be forgotten, but they carry a unique irreversibility risk that knowledge factors do not: if a password database leaks, the fix is a password reset; if a fingerprint template leaks, the user cannot grow a new fingerprint.

True multi-factor authentication requires combining factors from at least two different categories. A password plus a security question is still purely knowledge-based and provides essentially no additional protection against a determined attacker who has already compromised one secret, a distinction the exam tests directly.

slides.title: Why Offline Cracking Is the Real Threat Model
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Frames the entire technical section, everything from bcrypt to Argon2id exists specifically to defend the offline threat model.

Misconception: Students think rate limiting on the login page is sufficient password protection. It only protects the online attack surface, which is a small fraction of real-world password compromise.

Analogy: A bank vault's timed lock (online defense) is useless once the safe itself has been stolen and the thief can work on it in a private workshop with no time pressure (offline attack).

Exam tip: Any question about 'why does hash algorithm choice matter if we already rate-limit login attempts' is testing this online/offline distinction directly.
bullets: Online attack: Guessing passwords directly against a live login form, slow, loud, rate-limited
Offline attack: Attacker already has stolen hashes and cracks them on their own hardware with no rate limit
Why breaches change everything: Once hashes are exfiltrated, IDS/firewalls/rate-limiting no longer apply at all
Hardware: GPU clusters and ASICs can compute billions of hash attempts per second offline
Consequence: Password storage design (the hash function itself) matters more than login-page defenses once a breach occurs

content_blocks: Two fundamentally different threat models exist for password attacks, and confusing them leads to weak defenses. An online attack tests guesses directly against a live login endpoint, where every attempt is visible to the server, subject to rate limiting, and can trigger account lockout or CAPTCHA, this is a slow, detectable attack surface that modern web applications defend well.

An offline attack begins after an attacker has already exfiltrated a database of password hashes, typically via a data breach. From that point forward, none of the server's live defenses apply at all, there is no rate limiter, no IDS, no lockout policy, because the attacker is no longer talking to the server. They run guesses entirely on their own hardware, and modern GPU clusters or purpose-built ASICs can attempt billions of candidate passwords per second against a weak hash function.

This asymmetry is why password storage, specifically, the choice of hash function, is a fundamentally more important control than any login-page rate limiter. A breach converts an online, defensible attack into an offline, essentially undefendable one unless the stored hash itself was deliberately engineered to be slow to compute.

slides.title: Why Fast Hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) Are Wrong for Passwords

quiz.question: Why is SHA-256, despite having no known collision attacks, still considered an inappropriate choice for password storage?
options: SHA-256 produces hashes that are too short to be secure
SHA-256 is computed so quickly that an attacker with a stolen hash database can attempt billions of password guesses per second
SHA-256 cannot process passwords longer than 8 characters
SHA-256 requires a hardware security module to compute
quiz.explanation: SHA-256's design goal is speed and low latency for integrity-checking use cases, which is precisely the wrong property for password storage. Its raw computational speed on modern GPUs allows offline attackers to test enormous numbers of candidate passwords per second against stolen hashes, regardless of the fact that SHA-256 itself has no known collision or preimage attacks.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Explains precisely why 'just use a strong hash function' is the wrong instinct, speed itself is the vulnerability for passwords specifically.

Misconception: Students think SHA-256 is 'secure enough' because it isn't cryptographically broken like MD5/SHA-1. It is unbroken but still unsuitable for passwords due to raw speed.

Analogy: A padlock that can be picked in one second by a skilled locksmith is 'unbroken' in the sense that it wasn't tampered with, but it's still the wrong lock for a bank vault.

Exam tip: Distinguish 'cryptographically broken' (MD5, SHA-1, collisions found) from 'unsuitable for passwords due to speed' (SHA-256, still fast, not broken).

MD5: Cryptographically broken (2004 collision attack); a GPU computes ~68 billion MD5 hashes/second
SHA-1: Broken for collisions (Google's SHAttered, 2017); LinkedIn's unsalted SHA-1 was cracked within 72 hours
SHA-256: Not broken cryptographically, but still catastrophically fast, billions/second on consumer GPUs
Core problem: A hash function designed to be fast for legitimate verification is equally fast for an attacker's guesses

content_blocks: MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-256 were engineered for a completely different job than password storage: verifying that a large file has not been corrupted or tampered with, where speed and low latency are the entire point. Computing a SHA-256 checksum of a multi-gigabyte file in milliseconds is a feature for integrity checking and a catastrophic liability for password storage, because an attacker verifying a guessed password against a stolen hash benefits from that exact same speed.

MD5 (1992) is additionally cryptographically broken in the collision-resistance sense, two different inputs can be found that produce the same hash, and a modern GPU can compute roughly 68 billion MD5 hashes per second, making any password hashed with it recoverable in practical time. SHA-1 (1995) suffered a similar fate: Google's 2017 SHAttered attack demonstrated a practical collision, and its speed on GPUs is comparable to MD5's, LinkedIn's 2012 breach, discussed later, used unsalted SHA-1 and was substantially cracked within 72 hours.

SHA-256 remains cryptographically unbroken as a general-purpose hash function, but it is still fundamentally the wrong tool for passwords: it computes so quickly that low-entropy passwords fall to brute force in milliseconds once the hash database is stolen. The fix is not a 'more secure' fast hash, it is a deliberately slow, key-stretching algorithm, covered next.

slides.title: Salting: Defeating Rainbow Tables
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Directly explains the mechanism behind the LinkedIn case study's rapid 72-hour crack time, no salting meant one rainbow table cracked millions of accounts at once.

Misconception: Students think the salt must be secret, like a second password. It is stored in plaintext; its job is uniqueness, not confidentiality.

Analogy: Two identical letters mailed in envelopes stamped with different, publicly visible tracking numbers, the tracking number (salt) doesn't hide the letter's content, it just makes each envelope individually trackable rather than interchangeable.

Exam tip: Know that salts are stored unencrypted alongside the hash and that their purpose is defeating precomputed/rainbow-table attacks by forcing per-account computation.
bullets: Rainbow table: A precomputed lookup table mapping common strings to their hash outputs
Without salt: Identical passwords across different users produce identical hashes, one table cracks everyone
Salt: A random, per-user value combined with the password BEFORE hashing
Effect: Two users with password 'password123' get completely different stored hashes
Not secret: The salt is stored alongside the hash in plaintext, its value only needs to be unique, not hidden

content_blocks: Because SHA-256('password123') always produces the exact same output, an attacker can precompute hashes for millions of common passwords once and store the results in a rainbow table, a reusable lookup structure that instantly reverses any unsalted hash matching a common password, regardless of which website or user it came from.

Salting defeats this by combining a random, unique value (the salt) with the password before hashing, so that hash(salt_A + "password123") and hash(salt_B + "password123") produce completely unrelated outputs even though the underlying password is identical. An attacker now needs a separate rainbow table for every distinct salt value in the database, with a properly random salt per user, this effectively forces the attacker back to computing hashes one guess at a time per account, exactly as if no precomputation had ever been possible.

A common misconception is that the salt itself must be kept secret. It does not, salts are stored in plaintext directly alongside the hash in the database. Their security value comes entirely from uniqueness and randomness, not secrecy; modern algorithms like bcrypt and Argon2id generate and embed a random salt automatically as part of their standard output format.

slides.title: Credential Stuffing: Weaponizing Password Reuse

quiz.question: What is the key distinction between a credential stuffing attack and a classic brute-force attack?
options: Credential stuffing only targets administrator accounts
Credential stuffing replays real username/password pairs leaked from an unrelated prior breach, rather than systematically guessing combinations
Brute force requires physical access to the server
Credential stuffing is always slower than brute force
quiz.explanation: Credential stuffing specifically reuses credentials known to be real from a separate, unrelated breach, betting on password reuse across services. Classic brute force instead systematically tests candidate combinations (dictionary words, patterns, or exhaustive character sets) without any guarantee they were ever real credentials anywhere.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Sets up both the log-analysis application slide and the Colonial Pipeline case study later in the topic.

Misconception: Students conflate credential stuffing with brute force. Stuffing uses real, previously-breached credentials; brute force guesses combinations that were never necessarily real passwords anywhere.

Analogy: Trying a master key you found on the ground at every door in the neighborhood, rather than picking each lock individually.

Exam tip: The defining tell in a scenario is 'leaked credentials from a prior unrelated breach', that phrase always signals credential stuffing, not brute force.
bullets: Definition: Replaying stolen username/password pairs from one breach against unrelated services
Exploits: The human habit of reusing the same password across multiple sites
Scale: Verizon DBIR 2024, credential stuffing accounts for roughly 24% of breaches
Distinct from brute force: Stuffing uses real leaked credentials, not guessed combinations
Automation: Botnets distribute attempts across thousands of IPs to evade per-IP rate limits

content_blocks: Credential stuffing does not guess passwords, it replays passwords that are already known to be real, harvested from an entirely different, unrelated breach. If a user's LinkedIn password leaked in 2012 and that same user reused the identical password on their bank's website, an attacker's automated script trying that exact pair against the bank's login form has a real chance of success, entirely independent of the bank's own security posture.

The attack's effectiveness rests purely on human password-reuse behavior, which remains extremely common despite decades of security-awareness messaging. Because the credentials are drawn from real breach dumps rather than dictionary guesses, success rates per attempt are dramatically higher than classic brute force, and the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report attributes roughly a quarter of all breaches to this technique.

Modern credential-stuffing campaigns are automated through botnets, networks of compromised machines, that distribute login attempts across thousands of source IP addresses, each making only a handful of attempts, specifically to stay under any single IP's rate-limiting threshold while still testing enormous credential lists in aggregate.

slides.title: The WebAuthn Challenge-Response Sequence
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This is the single most important mechanism slide in the topic, it is the technical foundation for every phishing-resistance claim made elsewhere in Unit 1.

Misconception: Students think WebAuthn is 'just biometrics.' The biometric or PIN only unlocks the local private key; the cryptographic origin-binding is what defeats phishing, independent of how the key was unlocked.

Analogy: A wax seal stamped not just with the sender's signet, but with the exact address it was sealed at, a forged address on the outside of the envelope doesn't match the seal's embedded record.

bullets: WebAuthn: W3C browser API (part of FIDO2) enabling passwordless, phishing-resistant authentication
Roles: Client browser, physical/platform authenticator, and the Relying Party (the server)
Flow: Server issues a random challenge -> browser records the current page's origin -> authenticator signs both
Key property: ClientDataJSON embeds the browser-verified origin inside the signed data itself
Verification: Server checks the signature AND that the embedded origin matches the registered one

content_blocks: WebAuthn authentication is a three-party protocol: the client browser, a physical or platform authenticator (a hardware key or a device's secure enclave), and the Relying Party, the server verifying identity. The Relying Party begins by sending a fresh random challenge to the browser. Critically, the browser itself, not the website's JavaScript, records the actual origin (scheme, hostname, port) of the page currently loaded, and packages both the challenge and this browser-verified origin into a structure called ClientDataJSON.

The authenticator signs a hash of this combined data using the private key generated specifically for this Relying Party during registration. Because the private key never leaves the authenticator device, and because the signed payload embeds the actual origin the browser observed, the server can verify two things simultaneously with one signature check: that the correct private key was used, and that the request genuinely originated from the exact domain that registered the credential in the first place.

This is a fundamentally different trust model from passwords, which carry no cryptographic binding to the site they're being typed into, a password works identically whether typed into the real site or a perfect visual clone. WebAuthn's origin binding makes that clone-immunity possible.

slides.title: bcrypt: The Exponential Work-Factor Cost Parameter

quiz.question: If raising bcrypt's cost parameter C from 12 to 13 changes the per-hash computation time from 350ms to approximately 700ms, what does this demonstrate about bcrypt's work factor?
options: The relationship between cost and time is linear, adding a fixed increment per step
The relationship is exponential, each increment of C doubles the number of Blowfish iterations and therefore the computation time
bcrypt's cost parameter only affects memory usage, not time
The doubling indicates a flaw in the bcrypt algorithm
quiz.explanation: bcrypt's iteration count equals 2^C, so incrementing C by exactly one doubles the total iterations and, correspondingly, the computation time, going from 350ms to roughly 700ms is the expected exponential behavior, not a bug. This exponential relationship is what makes bcrypt 'future-adaptable': administrators can restore original real-world cost as hardware speeds up simply by raising C.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Gives the precise mathematical mechanism behind 'why key-stretching works,' connecting directly to the ebook's exponential formula.

Misconception: Students think bcrypt is 'just SHA-256 done a few extra times.' The iteration count is exponential in the cost parameter and specifically targeted at Blowfish's key schedule, not a generic repeated hashing loop.

Analogy: A combination lock with a built-in delay after each wrong guess, the delay doesn't stop a legitimate owner who knows the combination, but it makes exhaustive guessing take impossibly long.

Exam tip: Memorize the formula Iterations = 2^C and that OWASP's 2024 minimum recommended cost is 12.
bullets: Origin: Provos & Mazières (1999), based on the Blowfish cipher
Work factor (cost) C: Controls how many Blowfish key-schedule iterations run before returning a hash
Formula: Iterations = 2^C, each increment of C doubles computation time
Practical numbers: C=10 ≈ 100ms, C=12 ≈ 350ms, C=14 ≈ 1.4 seconds per hash
Future-adaptable: As hardware speeds up, simply raising C restores the original computational cost

content_blocks: bcrypt's defining feature is a single tunable cost parameter, C, that controls the number of iterations of its internal Blowfish-based key-setup routine. The relationship is exponential: total iterations equal 2 raised to the power of C, so each single increment of C doubles the time required to compute one hash. At C=12, the current OWASP-recommended minimum, the algorithm performs 4,096 iterations, taking roughly 350 milliseconds on typical server hardware.

350 milliseconds is imperceptible to a legitimate user logging in once. But for an attacker attempting to crack a stolen hash by trying a billion candidate passwords, that same 350ms per attempt multiplies into a computational cost that is millions of times larger than an equivalent fast hash like SHA-256 would require, turning what would be a milliseconds-scale offline attack into one requiring years or centuries of compute time.

The design was explicitly named 'future-adaptable' by its authors: because computing hardware reliably gets faster over time (historically following something like Moore's Law), a fixed-cost hash function becomes progressively weaker every year even without any flaw being discovered. bcrypt sidesteps this by letting administrators simply raise C as hardware improves, restoring the original real-world computational cost without changing the algorithm itself.

slides.title: Argon2id: Memory-Hardness Against GPUs and ASICs
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Extends bcrypt's time-hardness with the additional memory-hardness dimension, and directly explains why OWASP now prefers Argon2id where available.

Misconception: Students think 'more memory used' just means 'slower,' conflating memory-hardness with time-hardness. Memory-hardness specifically defeats parallelization, which is a distinct benefit from raw per-attempt slowness.

Analogy: A test that requires each student to use an entire private classroom (memory) rather than sharing one large lecture hall, you can no longer cram thousands of test-takers into the same space at once.

Exam tip: Know all three parameters (m, t, p) and the specific OWASP 2024 numbers: m=65536, t=3, p=4.

Three parameters: Memory cost (m, in KiB), Time cost (t, passes), Parallelism (p, threads)
OWASP 2024 recommendation: m=65536 (64MB), t=3, p=4
Memory-hardness: Requires large, pseudo-randomly-accessed memory blocks, GPUs have huge core counts but limited shared memory bandwidth
Effect on GPUs: A GPU that could run thousands of parallel SHA-256 attempts can run only a handful of parallel Argon2id attempts limited by RAM

slides.speaker_notes:

Misconception: Students think 'more memory used' just means 'slower,' conflating memory-hardness with time-hardness. Memory-hardness specifically defeats parallelization, which is a distinct benefit from raw per-attempt slowness.

content_blocks: Argon2id, the hybrid variant of the algorithm that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition, adds a defense that bcrypt lacks: deliberate memory-hardness. Where bcrypt's cost is purely a function of computation time, Argon2id additionally forces each hash attempt to allocate and repeatedly access a large block of memory, specified by the memory-cost parameter m in KiB, with the OWASP-recommended 65,536 corresponding to 64 megabytes per single hash computation.

This matters because of a structural weakness in GPU architecture: GPUs achieve their raw speed through thousands of small, simple cores, but those cores share a comparatively limited pool of memory bandwidth. A fast hash function like SHA-256 needs almost no memory per attempt, so a GPU can run thousands of parallel attempts limited only by core count. Argon2id's 64MB-per-attempt requirement means a GPU with, say, 8GB of onboard memory can run only a small handful of parallel attempts before exhausting available RAM, collapsing the GPU's core-count advantage entirely.

The time-cost parameter t (number of passes over the memory) and parallelism p (independent lanes within a single hash computation, not across different password guesses) round out the tuning surface. Because purpose-built ASICs are economical specifically when a computation needs little memory, Argon2id's memory-hardness also makes dedicated cracking hardware far less cost-effective to build than it would be against a purely compute-bound algorithm.

It times a single SHA-256 computation against a loop that repeats hashing 2^12 = 4,096 times, mirroring bcrypt's iteration count at cost=12, and prints the ratio.

import hashlib, time

def fast_hash(pw):
    return hashlib.sha256(pw.encode()).hexdigest()

def stretched_hash(pw, cost=12):
    h = pw.encode()
    iterations = 2 ** cost
    for _ in range(iterations):
        h = hashlib.sha256(h).digest()
    return h.hex()

pw = 'CorrectHorseBatteryStaple'

t0 = time.perf_counter()
fast_hash(pw)
t_fast = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
stretched_hash(pw, cost=12)
t_stretched = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f'Fast SHA-256:        {t_fast*1000:.4f} ms')
print(f'Stretched (2^12x):   {t_stretched*1000:.2f} ms')
print(f'Ratio:                {t_stretched/t_fast:.0f}x slower')
print(f'\nAt 1 billion guesses:')
print(f'  Fast hash total time:      {t_fast*1e9/3600:.1f} hours')
print(f'  Stretched hash total time: {t_stretched*1e9/3600/24/365:.1f} years')

content_blocks: Detecting credential stuffing in raw authentication logs is a pattern-recognition task across several independently weak signals. The signature pattern is a high volume of failed logins spread across many distinct usernames and many distinct source IP addresses, where no single IP or username individually crosses a naive rate-limiting threshold, this is precisely the distributed structure that a botnet is designed to produce.

Two secondary signals sharpen the diagnosis. Automation scripts frequently reuse the exact same User-Agent header across every request, since a bot rarely bothers to randomize this field unless specifically engineered to; real human traffic naturally shows far more device and browser diversity. Similarly, genuine human login attempts show natural timing variance, while scripted attacks often show suspiciously uniform intervals between requests, a fixed delay baked into the attack tooling.

No single signal alone is conclusive: a legitimate spike in traffic, a shared corporate NAT IP, or a common browser extension could each individually produce one of these patterns innocently. The analyst's actual skill is correlating multiple weak signals into a confident verdict, the same defense-in-depth-of-evidence principle introduced for phishing detection in Topic 1.1.

quiz.question: Why does the Have I Been Pwned Pwned Passwords API only require the client to send the first 5 characters of a password's SHA-1 hash, rather than the full hash?
options: 5 characters is the maximum length the API can process
Sending only a short hash prefix preserves k-anonymity, the API returns all matches for that prefix, and the client compares locally without ever revealing the full password or hash
SHA-1 hashes longer than 5 characters are not unique
The API compresses the hash to save bandwidth only
quiz.explanation: This is a k-anonymity privacy design: transmitting only a short hash prefix means the request is ambiguous among hundreds of thousands of possible passwords sharing that prefix. The API returns all matching suffixes for that prefix, and the actual full-hash comparison happens entirely on the client's own device, so the operator of the API never learns which specific password the user actually checked.

content_blocks: NIST SP 800-63B recommends that authentication systems check candidate passwords against databases of previously breached credentials at registration and password-change time, rejecting known-compromised passwords outright regardless of how 'complex' they appear. Have I Been Pwned, maintained by security researcher Troy Hunt, is the most widely used such database, aggregating well over 14 billion breached account records.

Implementing this check naively would require sending the user's actual password, or even its full hash, to a third-party API, which is itself a serious privacy and security risk; a compromised or malicious API could harvest every password checked against it. HIBP's Pwned Passwords API solves this with k-anonymity: the client computes the SHA-1 hash of the candidate password locally, then sends only the first five hexadecimal characters of that hash to the API.

The API responds with every known breached hash suffix that shares that same five-character prefix, typically several hundred entries, and the client compares its own full hash locally against that returned list. The full password and its full hash never leave the user's device at all; only a broad, ambiguous five-character prefix is transmitted, shared by hundreds of thousands of other possible hashes, making it impossible for the API operator to determine which specific password was actually checked.

slides.title: Case Study: The 2012 LinkedIn Unsalted SHA-1 Breach

quiz.question: Explain why the absence of salting was the specific technical failure that allowed 90% of LinkedIn's leaked password hashes to be cracked within 72 hours, and describe the fix.
quiz.prompt: Address what salting would have changed about the identical-password-identical-hash problem.
quiz.explanation: Without salting, SHA-1 hashing is fully deterministic: any two accounts sharing the identical password produce byte-for-byte identical stored hashes, regardless of which accounts they belong to. This allowed attackers to precompute a single rainbow table mapping common passwords to their SHA-1 hashes once, and then instantly reverse any matching stolen hash across the entire database with essentially zero per-account computational cost, explaining the extremely fast 72-hour crack time. Had LinkedIn applied a unique, random salt per user before hashing, two users with the identical password would have produced completely unrelated stored hashes, forcing an attacker to mount a separate computational attack per individual account rather than reusing one precomputed table across the whole breach, this alone would have increased cracking cost by many orders of magnitude, even before considering key-stretching (bcrypt/Argon2id).

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The definitive real-world illustration of the salting mechanism slide, connect the two directly when teaching.

Misconception: Students assume a breach's damage is fully known at initial disclosure. LinkedIn's true scope was 18x larger and surfaced years later.

Analogy: A single master key that happens to open every door with the same identical lock model, find one key, unlock every matching door instantly.

Exam tip: Cite this case specifically when asked to justify salting as a mandatory (not optional) password-storage control.

Within 72 hours of the breach becoming public, security researchers and attackers alike had cracked over 90% of the leaked hashes, exposing widespread simple-password use and rampant password reuse across other services.

The full scope of the breach was dramatically understated at first disclosure. It emerged in 2016 that the true number of compromised accounts was not 6.5 million but 117 million, the additional 110 million records surfaced on dark web markets four years later, still enabling credential-stuffing attacks against users who had never changed their now-ancient but still-valid password.

slides.title: Case Study: Colonial Pipeline (2021), A Single Reused Password

quiz.question: What single control, if enabled on the Colonial Pipeline VPN account, would most directly have stopped the credential-stuffing login even though the correct password was used?
options: A longer minimum password length policy
Multi-factor authentication, since a correct password alone would then be insufficient to complete login
A stronger encryption cipher for the VPN tunnel
Rate limiting on the company's public website
quiz.explanation: Because the attacker used a genuinely correct, previously-leaked password (not a guessed one), password-policy changes would not have prevented this specific login. MFA would have required a second, independent factor (possession or inherence) that the attacker did not possess, blocking access even with the correct password in hand, this is exactly why the FBI's report highlighted the absence of MFA as the pivotal missing control.

content_blocks: In May 2021, Colonial Pipeline, operator of the largest refined petroleum pipeline system in the United States, suffered a ransomware attack whose root cause traced back to a single compromised VPN account. Investigators determined the account's password had been exposed years earlier in a completely unrelated public data breach, and the employee had reused that same password for the company VPN.

The VPN account had no multi-factor authentication enabled, so possession of the correct password alone, obtained through straightforward credential stuffing against a public breach dump, was sufficient for the attacker to gain network access. From that foothold, the DarkSide ransomware-as-a-service group encrypted the company's billing and operational technology systems, forcing a complete multi-day operational shutdown and triggering fuel shortages across the US East Coast. Colonial ultimately paid a $4.4 million Bitcoin ransom, of which the FBI later recovered roughly $2.3 million.

The FBI's post-incident analysis is a textbook defense-in-depth failure case: the account had no MFA, the VPN enforced no geolocation or IP restrictions, and no behavioral anomaly detection flagged the anomalous login. Any single one of these three independent controls, a free authenticator app being the cheapest, would very likely have prevented the entire chain of national-scale consequences.

Where Argon2id is unavailable, bcrypt with a cost factor of at least 12 remains an excellent, battle-tested fallback used by default in many major web frameworks.

Any system still hashing passwords with MD5, unsalted SHA-1, or bare SHA-256 has a critical, immediately actionable finding: none of these are acceptable for credential storage regardless of any other compensating control, and migration should be treated as urgent.

Migrating a live system away from a legacy hash function presents a practical challenge: you cannot recover a user's plaintext password from its old hash to re-hash it with the new algorithm. The standard, low-risk migration pattern is lazy re-hashing, verify the user's password against the old hash one final time at their next successful login (since the plaintext is briefly available at that moment), then immediately compute and store a new hash using the modern algorithm, retiring the old hash for that account. Accounts that never log in again over time can be handled with a forced password reset.

slides.speaker_notes:

Misconception: Students think rate limiting by IP alone is sufficient. A distributed credential-stuffing botnet specifically defeats single-IP-only limiting; per-username tracking is also required.

content_blocks: The token bucket algorithm models rate limiting as a bucket that continuously fills with tokens at a fixed rate and drains one token per incoming request; a request is only allowed through if a token is currently available, and requests are rejected or delayed once the bucket is empty. Its key advantage over a simple fixed-window counter is graceful burst tolerance: a user who mistypes their password twice in quick succession is not unfairly blocked, since the bucket can hold several tokens at once, while sustained high-volume abuse still drains the bucket and gets throttled.

For login endpoints specifically, effective configurations track two separate buckets simultaneously: one keyed by source IP (catching a single attacker hammering many accounts from one machine) and one keyed by target username (catching a distributed botnet credential-stuffing attempt against one specific high-value account from many different IPs). Relying on only one of these misses the other attack shape entirely, exactly the asymmetry credential stuffing is designed to exploit.

Rate limiting alone is rarely the final control; mature implementations pair it with exponential backoff (each successive failure imposing a longer delay before the next attempt is accepted) and, after repeated violations, a CAPTCHA challenge or temporary account lockout, escalating the friction imposed specifically on the party currently failing to authenticate.

slides.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Modern Password Policy Guidance

quiz.question: According to NIST SP 800-63B's current guidance, which password policy change is recommended in place of mandatory periodic password rotation?
options: Requiring a password change every 30 days instead of 90
Real-time screening of candidate passwords against known-breached password databases, combined with prioritizing length over composition complexity
Requiring all passwords to include at least one special character
Eliminating password-based authentication for all systems immediately

content_blocks: NIST SP 800-63B's 2020 revision reversed decades of conventional password-policy wisdom based on empirical research into how humans actually respond to rules. content_blocks: As with Topic 1.1's phishing scenarios, precisely distinguishing detection from mitigation is a recurring exam requirement in authentication contexts. A detection control observes and reports that something suspicious is happening, a SOC rule that alerts when the four credential-stuffing signals (high username distribution, many IPs, identical User-Agent, uniform timing) co-occur is a detective control; it tells an analyst an attack is in progress but does not, by itself, stop a single login attempt.

Rate limiting a login endpoint by IP and username actively blocks excess attempts; requiring MFA means a correctly guessed or stuffed password is insufficient to complete login; and storing passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt means that even a successful database breach yields hashes that resist offline cracking for a practically infeasible amount of time.

Scenario-based free-response questions in this unit almost always ask for both categories explicitly, a detective control that surfaces the incident for analyst review, and a preventive/mitigating control that reduces or eliminates the actual damage, and conflating the two, or naming only one, costs partial credit.

slides.title: Incident Response Walkthrough: The Sunbelt Retail Login Spike

quiz.question: Given an overnight spike of 40,000 failed logins across 12,000 usernames from 3,000 IPs, all sharing an identical User-Agent and uniform ~180ms timing, (a) identify the attack and justify from the evidence, (b) name two distinct mitigations, and (c) describe one detective SOC rule.
quiz.prompt: Separate a control that blocks the current attack from one that limits future breach damage; separate both from a detective rule.
quiz.explanation: (a) This is a distributed credential-stuffing attack: the high number of distinct target usernames combined with a comparably high number of distinct source IPs indicates automation spreading attempts to evade per-account and per-IP thresholds, and the identical User-Agent plus uniform timing indicate scripted, non-human traffic rather than organic user error. (b) Two valid mitigations: (1) tighten IP- and username-keyed token-bucket rate limiting, with CAPTCHA/step-up verification triggered for traffic matching this signature, to throttle the current flood; (2) ensure all credentials are stored with Argon2id or bcrypt and that MFA is enforced organization-wide, so that even a successful stuffed login attempt cannot complete without a second factor, and any future breach of the credential database resists offline cracking. (c) A detective SOC rule: alert when failed-login attempts against a high count of distinct usernames exceed a defined threshold within a short time window while User-Agent diversity remains abnormally low, correlating source IPs into a shared incident and feeding them into an IP-reputation blocklist.

slides.title: Common Misconception: 'A Complex Password Is Enough'

quiz.question: A user chooses an extremely long, complex, unique password for a banking site. The bank, however, stores it using unsalted MD5, and separately the user's identical password was leaked from an unrelated breach years earlier. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The password's complexity fully protects the account regardless of the bank's storage method or reuse

The password's complexity offers no protection here, if it was reused and leaked, credential stuffing succeeds regardless of complexity, and MD5 storage additionally exposes it to offline cracking if breached
MD5 storage is irrelevant as long as the password is complex enough
Complexity only matters for online brute-force attacks, which is the only relevant threat in this scenario
quiz.explanation: Password complexity has no bearing on credential stuffing, since the attacker already possesses the exact leaked string and does not need to guess anything, reuse alone defeats complexity. Separately, unsalted MD5 storage means the bank's own database, if breached, is vulnerable to rainbow-table and brute-force cracking regardless of how complex the underlying password was. Complexity is a real but narrow defense against online/offline guessing of a password that was never reused or leaked, it is not a substitute for uniqueness or for the server's own storage practices.

Complexity is equally irrelevant to server-side storage failures entirely outside the user's control: an extremely complex password hashed with a fast, unsalted algorithm on a poorly engineered server can still be recovered via rainbow tables or brute force at scale, exactly as happened to some LinkedIn accounts in 2012 regardless of how strong the underlying password had been.

The accurate mental model treats password strength, password uniqueness across sites, the server's storage algorithm, and the presence of MFA as four largely independent variables, each defending against a different specific failure mode. A user can maximize the one variable fully within their control, never reusing a password, and enabling MFA wherever offered, while having zero influence over how a given service stores that password server-side.

slides.title: Synthesis: Salt, Pepper, Work Factor, and Entropy Together

quiz.question: A company's user database is breached, exposing all password hashes and per-user salts, but NOT the application's separate secrets manager. Passwords were hashed with bcrypt at a high work factor. Which layer of defense still stands, and why?
choices: None, salt and work factor are both defeated once the database is breached

The pepper still protects the hashes, since it's stored outside the database specifically to survive a database-only breach; the high work factor also still slows any cracking attempt against the exposed hashes
Only entropy protects the hashes now
Authorization prevents the attacker from using the stolen hashes
quiz.explanation: Pepper is deliberately stored OUTSIDE the database (in a secrets manager or application code) precisely so a database-only breach doesn't expose it, without the pepper, an attacker can't correctly compute candidate hashes even with the salts. The work factor independently still slows any cracking attempt regardless of what was stolen.

content_blocks: This slide consolidates the vocabulary pairs the assessment tests with precision. A salt is a per-user random value, stored in plaintext alongside its hash, whose job is uniqueness; a pepper is a related but distinct concept, a single secret value applied to every password in the system and stored separately from the database itself (often in application code or a secrets manager), adding protection specifically against a database-only breach that doesn't also expose the application's secret store.

Hashing and encryption are frequently confused: hashing is a deliberately one-way transformation appropriate for passwords, since the system only ever needs to verify a match, never recover the original; encryption is reversible given the correct key, appropriate for data the system genuinely needs to read back later, such as stored credit card numbers.

Work factor describes how expensive the hash algorithm itself makes each individual guess (a property of bcrypt/Argon2id configuration); entropy describes how many guesses are needed in the first place (a property of the password's own length and randomness), both matter, and confusing them is a common source of missed points.

slides.title: Synthesis: The Full Credential Lifecycle Attack Chain

quiz.question: In the credential lifecycle chain (creation -> storage -> breach -> weaponization -> unauthorized access), which single control remains effective at the FINAL link even if every earlier link in the chain has already failed?
options: A longer minimum password length policy at the original breached service
Multi-factor authentication at the victim service, since it requires a factor beyond the stolen password regardless of how the password was obtained
Salting at the originally breached service
Rate limiting at the originally breached service
quiz.explanation: Salting and strong hashing address the storage/breach links at the ORIGINAL service, and rate limiting slows the weaponization attempt, but if all of those have already failed and the attacker possesses a valid, correct username/password pair, MFA at the victim service is the only control positioned at the final link, requiring a second independent factor the attacker does not have regardless of how the password was ultimately obtained.

content_blocks: The Colonial Pipeline case study is best understood not as an isolated event but as the final link of a chain that began years earlier and elsewhere entirely. A password is created, often reused across multiple services out of human convenience. It is stored by whichever service the user registered with, either securely (salted, key-stretched) or insecurely (a fast, unsalted hash) depending entirely on that service's engineering choices, invisible to the user.

If that service is later breached, as LinkedIn was in 2012, the stored hashes are exfiltrated, and if storage was weak, offline cracking recovers the actual plaintext password within hours or days. That recovered username/password pair then becomes ammunition for an entirely unrelated attack years later and elsewhere: credential stuffing against any other service where the same user reused the same password, as occurred against Colonial Pipeline's VPN.

Mapping defenses to the specific link they sever clarifies why layered defense matters: strong storage (Argon2id/bcrypt with salting) at the original service prevents step 3 from ever succeeding even after a breach; rate limiting at the victim service slows step 4's automated attempts; and MFA at the victim service breaks the chain's final link entirely, rendering a perfectly correct stolen password insufficient on its own regardless of every earlier failure in the chain.

content_blocks: Use this checklist to self-assess before the assessment. Each item maps to a high-frequency question pattern for this topic. The two concepts most likely to determine full versus partial credit are (1) precisely explaining why key-stretched, memory-hard hashing (bcrypt/Argon2id) is necessary specifically because of the offline-cracking threat model, not merely as a generically 'stronger' algorithm, and (2) correctly distinguishing credential stuffing (reused real leaked credentials) from brute force (guessed combinations) using the specific log-pattern evidence, high username/IP distribution, identical User-Agent, uniform timing.

Beyond those, expect at least one item testing the salt-versus-pepper or hashing-versus-encryption vocabulary pairs precisely, and at least one free-response item requiring the full five-layer authentication hardening stack (storage, salting, rate limiting, breach screening, MFA) rather than a single named control.

Finally, keep the detection-versus-mitigation distinction sharp, exactly as in Topic 1.1: a SOC alert rule detects an ongoing credential-stuffing campaign; Argon2id, rate limiting, and MFA are what actually mitigate it. Scenario prompts almost always require naming both categories explicitly.

big_idea.text: A spoofed login page is a fake teller's window set up right next to the real one at the bank. It looks identical to the customer standing in line — but the money, in this case your credentials, goes into a completely different vault.
big_idea.closing: Hold onto this picture — we'll come back to it as the mechanics get more technical.
